notes: Complete libel preliminary issues judgment on non-justiciability and stay.

enrichment.short_title: Libel stay where bishop-consecration defence raises non-justiciable religious issues
key_facts: Jonathan Blake, a former Church of England vicar who left in 1994 and was later consecrated bishop within POEM/SICM, sued the Daily Mail over articles describing him as a self-styled or imitation bishop after he officiated at a televised same-sex blessing.
Associated Newspapers pleaded justification and fair comment disputing the validity of his episcopal status and alleging masquerade as a Church of England-style bishop.

Both sides accepted that doctrinal and ecclesiastical questions about valid consecration and apostolic succession were non-justiciable; the issue was whether the libel action could proceed in adapted form or must be stayed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issues in a Queen's Bench libel action on whether non-justiciable defences require a stay of the whole claim.
enrichment.outcome: Action stayed; the court held non-justiciable issues were central to justification and fair comment and could not be fairly tried or sufficiently tailored without infringing Article 10.
enrichment.ratio: Where defences of justification and fair comment in a libel action necessarily require the court to adjudicate doctrinal, procedural and fitness questions about religious office that the court will not enter, the action must be stayed even though the claimant is thereby denied vindication; a stay should be granted only in extreme cases but is required when excluded issues are not marginal and cannot be excised without unfairly restricting the defendant's freedom of expression.
legal_issues: Scope of non-justiciability in disputes over religious status and doctrine
Whether a libel claim can proceed if core justification issues are non-justiciable
Interaction of stay with Article 9 and Article 10 ECHR
Whether a secular historical-fact formulation avoids non-justiciability

enrichment.short_title: Proprietary estoppel after caring for alcoholic partner; £50k award upheld

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

key_facts: Dorothy Ottey lived with Timothy Andreae from 1996 to October 1999, caring for him through severe alcoholism; he promised her a Jamaica flat outright and a life interest in his Chelsea houseboat in a 1998 letter of intent.

The estate (~£1.5m) was left on discretionary trusts excluding her; the judge upheld partial proprietary estoppel (£50,000 plus transfer of the Jamaica apartment or £50,000) but rejected her 1975 Act claim.
The executor appealed on promise, detriment, reliance and quantum; Ottey cross-appealed for full expectation (~£250,000).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a Chancery deputy judge's trial decision on proprietary estoppel and a failed 1975 Act claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; proprietary estoppel established and the £50,000 plus Jamaica apartment order affirmed as proportionate.
enrichment.ratio: Proprietary estoppel requires assurances, detrimental reliance and unconscionability assessed in the round; reliance may be inferred from express promises and the burden shifts to the promisor to disprove it; remedy must be proportionate to detriment and expectation, so specific testamentary promises need not be fulfilled in full where the relationship ended before death and expectation exceeded detriment.
legal_issues: Whether quasi-matrimonial testamentary promises survive relationship breakdown
Detriment and reliance where care overlapped ordinary cohabitation
Appropriate equitable remedy under Jennings v Rice
Relationship between 1975 Act assessment and estoppel relief

enrichment.short_title: Anglian Water sewage discharge fine reduced from £200,000 to £60,000
key_facts: About 200 tonnes of polluted sewage effluent entered the river Crouch from Wickford Sewage Treatment Works after a gate bolt de-threaded and a turbidity safety monitor was away for repair.
Anglian Water pleaded guilty to a strict-liability section 85(3) offence; the Crown Court fined £200,000; dead fish were observed over two kilometres though the river recovered within 24 hours.
The company had many prior pollution convictions but argued the fine was manifestly excessive given limited spatial/temporal impact and strict liability without deliberate corner-cutting.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Sentence appeal to the Court of Appeal with leave after conviction in the Crown Court following committal from magistrates.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; fine reduced to £60,000; defendant's costs order granted.
enrichment.ratio: Strict-liability environmental offences carry a heavy preventive burden and culpability findings matter, but fines must reflect gravity, impact, compliance history and means; a fail-safe system should have been in place, yet a £200,000 fine for this single local incident was manifestly excessive compared with comparable authorities.
legal_issues: Appropriate level of fine for strict-liability water pollution
Role of culpability where mens rea is not required
Impact of extensive prior convictions
Sentencing principles for regulated monopoly undertakers

enrichment.short_title: JR succeeds against 42nd horserace levy on betting exchanges as procedurally unfair
key_facts: Sporting Options, a new betting exchange, challenged the Horserace Betting Levy Board's 42nd levy scheme requiring 10% of gross profits of successful layers on British racing with no loss offsets, replacing the prior 10%-of-commission basis.
The Bookmakers' Committee recommended the change amid concern that exchanges were reducing traditional bookmakers' levy yield; consultation with exchanges was limited and late.
The claimant undertook to pay levy on the old commission basis pending litigation; only declaratory relief was pursued.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Board's 31 October 2002 levy decision, with permission limited to declaratory relief subject to an undertaking on payment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the decision to adopt the betting-exchange provisions was unlawful and manifestly unfair; declaratory relief granted (decision would have been quashed but for the relief limitation).
enrichment.ratio: In setting the horserace betting levy the Board was obliged to consult betting exchanges fairly while proposals remained formative, give adequate reasons and time, and conscientiously consider responses; failure to consult Sporting Options properly, combined with misleading uncorrected minutes and inadequate opportunity to assess economic impact, rendered the October 2002 decision procedurally unfair.
legal_issues: Duty to consult betting exchanges before adopting levy changes
Procedural fairness under Coughlan principles
Whether levy basis change from commission to layers' profits was substantively irrational
Status of betting exchanges as bookmakers under the 1963 Act

notes: Complete test-case judgment on section 55 asylum support and Article 3.

enrichment.short_title: Section 55 late asylum claims: Article 3 requires support despite s55(1) refusal
key_facts: Three test claimants (S, D, T) were refused asylum support under section 55 because they did not claim asylum at the airport as soon as reasonably practicable after arrival.
After support withdrawal they slept rough, begged for food and suffered malnutrition, humiliation and deteriorating health while awaiting asylum decisions.
D's section 55(1) refusal was quashed as irrational; S and T failed on section 55(1) but all three succeeded under section 55(5)/Article 3.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review test cases challenging section 55 asylum support refusals.
enrichment.outcome: Mixed on section 55(1): D succeeded, S and T failed; all three succeeded on Article 3; declarations that support was required to avoid inhuman or degrading treatment.
enrichment.ratio: Section 55(1) requires an individualised assessment of whether asylum was claimed as soon as reasonably practicable, having regard to agents and the claimant's state of mind; where refusal of support reduces a destitute asylum seeker to a condition verging on the Article 3 severity described in Pretty v UK, section 55(5) obliges the Secretary of State to provide support to avoid inhuman or degrading treatment.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'as soon as reasonably practicable' under section 55(1)
Procedural fairness after R (Q) v SSHD
When destitution engages Article 3 ECHR
Interaction of section 55(5) with interim relief

enrichment.short_title: Iraqi bank denied extension to appeal registration of Dutch judgment
key_facts: Citibank registered a Dutch default judgment for ~US$11.4m against Iraqi state banks Rasheed and Rafidian under the Brussels Convention/CJJA 1982.
Rasheed applied over a year late to extend time to appeal registration, citing UN sanctions preventing payment of legal fees and Article 6 fair trial rights.
Service of the registration order was effected in March 2002; sanctions ended in May 2003; Treasury had rejected repeated applications to release frozen funds for legal fees.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under CPR Part 3.1 and 52.6 to extend time to file an appellant's notice against registration of a foreign judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused on discretion despite jurisdiction to extend; extension of time denied.
enrichment.ratio: CPR Part 3.1(2)(a) can extend time to appeal registration even after expiry, but relief under Part 3.9 requires prompt application and good explanation; intentional delay, failure to file a protective appellant's notice, and availability of non-frozen funds meant finality and Citibank's enforcement interests outweighed Rasheed's late Article 6 challenge.
legal_issues: Jurisdiction to extend Brussels Convention appeal time under CPR Part 74.8 and Part 3.1
Effect of UN/Iraq sanctions on Article 6 access to justice
Discretion under CPR Part 3.9
Whether public policy/Article 6 can be raised on registration appeal

enrichment.short_title: Special removal of old on-licence to Gresham Hotel: JR dismissed
key_facts: Ultimate Leisure sought special removal of Mim's Bar old on-licence (continuous since 1872) to the Gresham Hotel in Jesmond after failed full-licence applications amid police and residents' objections to disorder and noise on Osborne Road.
Residents judicially reviewed Newcastle licensing justices' rejection of abuse-of-process, ECHR and planning adjournment arguments.
The justices had improperly begun hearing the application after posting a notice that the hearing was adjourned.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of preliminary rulings in licensing justices proceedings on special removal under sections 12 and 15 of the Licensing Act 1964.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on all grounds; abuse of process, ECHR incompatibility, planning adjournment and wide construction of 'premises' challenges rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Using the special removal procedure to avoid objections available on a full on-licence application is not an abuse of process where the applicant lawfully relies on statutory rights; Article 6 is engaged but sections 12 and 15 remain proportionate because Article 8 and Protocol 1 rights can be protected by closure, revocation, nuisance and environmental remedies; 'premises' means buildings and does not extend to external site areas on this application.
legal_issues: Abuse of process in special removal applications
Article 6 fairness where Article 8 and Protocol 1 rights are affected
Proportionality of limited grounds for refusing special removal
Whether planning consent must be resolved before licensing decision
Meaning of 'premises' in section 12(4)(b)

enrichment.short_title: Barnstaple bypass: estuary not treated as constructive SPA on appeal
key_facts: Devon County Council's Western Bypass of Barnstaple included a bridge across the Taw and Torridge Estuary; objectors argued the estuary should be treated as a Special Protection Area under the Wild Birds Directive.
The estuary appeared on earlier potential SPA lists (1988-1992) but was omitted from PPG9 Annex B in 1994; current ornithological data did not meet SPA selection guidelines.
Following a public inquiry the Secretary of State confirmed the scheme; Collins J dismissed the challenge and the appeal was expedited.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law from dismissal of a highways/compulsory purchase challenge relating to SPA status.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no requirement to treat the estuary as an SPA or constructive SPA for the 2002 decision.
enrichment.ratio: A site listed as a potential SPA in the past does not permanently bind the state as if classified; classification decisions must be based on current ornithological evidence and formal procedure, and it is too late to challenge the 1994 removal from the official list; where current data show the estuary does not meet SPA criteria, the Secretary of State was entitled to proceed on that basis.
legal_issues: Legal effect of historic potential SPA designation
Whether unclassified suitable sites must be treated as SPAs under ECJ case law
Lawfulness of de-designation or removal from potential SPA lists
Application of IBA 89 and JNCC selection guidelines

enrichment.short_title: Tower crane collapse: climbing held erection under CPA Conditions 13(c)(ii)
key_facts: Tower crane TC3 collapsed during a weekend climbing operation at HSBC's Canary Wharf headquarters site, causing fatalities, injuries and large delay claims (~£16.6m).
Yarm Road hired the crane from Hewden under an order incorporating CPA model conditions; preliminary issues concerned allocation of loss under clauses 8, 11 and 13.
Climbing added mast sections using Hewden's specialist team after Yarm installed and welded tie supports; the collapse occurred after ties were certified.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal on preliminary contractual issues after Technology and Construction Court trial of issues 1-5.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed by majority (2:1); Hewden liable under clause 13(c)(ii) for erection during exclusive-control climbing; Yarm's KCB indemnity clause did not override CPA allocation.
enrichment.ratio: On the majority view, extending a tower crane by climbing is 'erection of plant' within CPA clause 13(c)(ii) even if not the initial erection, and the actual climbing phase after handover was under Hewden's exclusive control; clause 13(b) hirer indemnity therefore does not apply, and the general KCB clause 11 indemnity yields to the specific CPA conditions.
legal_issues: Whether crane climbing is 'erection' under CPA clause 13(c)(ii)
Exclusive control during climbing versus preparatory tie works
Effect of clause 8 deeming operators servants of hirer
Whether Yarm's standard indemnity clause 11 prevails over CPA clause 13

enrichment.short_title: Supported housing use held Class C3 after adequate council investigation

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987

key_facts: ECHG used three adjoining terraced houses on Broadway, Kettering to accommodate up to six vulnerable young people per house with support workers.
Mrs Hossack challenged the council's October 2002 decision that each house was a separate Class C3 dwelling rather than a sui generis hostel use requiring planning permission.
Following Court of Appeal guidance in Hossack [2002] EWCA Civ 886, the council reinvestigated via site inspection, records review and interview with ECHG's senior housing officer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Kettering Borough Council's redetermination of use class following remittal from the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; council's Class C3 decision and refusal to reconsider were rational; no requirement for wider resident/neighbour interviews.
enrichment.ratio: Whether supported housing falls within Class C3 is primarily a planning judgment reviewable only for Wednesbury irrationality; after applying Barnes/Rogers/Simmons factors and the Court of Appeal's Hossack guidance, a council may reasonably conclude that up to six residents in each house live as a single household where communal living is evidenced, even if neighbour witness statements describe disorder.

Adequacy of council investigation before use-class determination
Application of Hossack CA guidance on relationship between residents
Whether three adjoining houses form one planning unit
